content: Dr. Peilong Li is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Elizabethtown College, where he has been on the faculty since 2018. He currently serves as the Program Director of Computer Science. Prior to joining Etown, Dr. Li was a Research Assistant Professor at University of Massachusetts Lowell, where he also received his Ph.D. in Computer Engineering in 2015. His research applies machine learning to cybersecurity, including malware and network traffic analysis, edge AI and IoT systems, large language models and conversational agents, and privacy-preserving learning, with applications in health and education. He has received research grants from funding agencies including the National Science Foundation, Intel and Google, and his work has been cited over 2,000 times (Google Scholar h-index 15). He has also established the Agentic and Dependable AI Lab (ADAL) for undergraduate student research at the college.

Course Coverage Network Security is a comprehensive hands-on course designed for IT professionals, network administrators, and anyone interested in enhancing their network security skills. Covering a broad spectrum of topics, from the basics of networking and TCP protocols to advanced topics such as firewall implementation and security, virtual private networks, and DNS attacks and protection, this course equips students with the knowledge and skills required to defend against network threats.  Foundational Understanding: Grasp networking security fundamentals, including the protocol layers, packet sniffing and spoofing, and the use of tools such as Scapy and Wireshark. Red and Blue Teaming: Identify and simulate network threats in each protocol layer as a Red Team, and develop defense strategies as a Blue Team. Practical Application: Implement high-level security applications, from firewall setups to VPN configurations, to shield networks from vulnerabilities. Collaborative Learning: Present a network security project, applying course knowledge and receiving peer feedback. Competitive Skill Assessment: Participate in ‘Capture the Flag’ competitions, applying knowledge to identify and defend network vulnerabilities.

All projects and assignments must be completed by students individually, without assistance from anyone other than the instructor. Students can discuss the course material with each other at a conceptual level, but each student must do his or her own work. For projects, exams, and all other activities in the course, students are expected to act according to the official policy on academic dishonesty and the highest standards of personal integrity.
The first infraction of academic honesty in this course will carry a penalty of a 0 for the project, lab, or exam in question and a reduction of a full letter grade in the final grade. If a second infraction occurs, the students involved will fail the course, and the instructor will seek the maximum penalty possible under the college’s regulations, up to and including expulsion.

You will be turned away from class if you do not have a face covering. Students diagnosed with a health condition that precludes mask wearing can contact Lynne Davies in Disability Services (daviesl@etown.edu) to request remote learning as a reasonable accommodation.
If you are exhibiting any symptoms of COVID or fail to pass the daily health screen, do not come to class. Failure to adhere to the established community expectations around safety will result in notification of Campus Security and application of the student conduct process for failure to comply, endangering the well-being of others, and/or disorderly conduct. The student code of conduct applies also to participation in all virtual activities, including Zoom sessions and discussion boards

Therefore, your instructor will consider it a violation of academic integrity to use a GenAI tool for any purpose that is not explicitly outlined in assignment instructions. While this new technology can be very useful in certain contexts, it is important to make sure that its usage in the classroom setting is limited in order to ensure that you are doing original work and developing your critical thinking skills. In circumstances in which AI usage is permitted in class, you must acknowledge that usage and provide the chatbot with credit when it is a cited source. For instance, to cite ChatGPT in APA, the APA provides some direction at https://apastyle.apa.org/blog/how-to-cite-chatgpt. If you have any questions or uncertainty over the use of AI in this course, please reach out to the instructor.
Respect for Diversity It is my intent that students from all backgrounds and perspectives be well served by this course, that students’ learning needs be addressed both in and out of class, and that the diversity that students bring to this class be viewed as a resource, strength, and benefit. I also intend to present materials and activities that respect diversity: gender, sexuality, disability, age, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, race, and culture. Please let me know if there are ways to further serve the diverse needs you or other students may have.
Religious Observances The College is eager to facilitate individual religious beliefs and practices whenever possible while retaining course student learning outcomes. It is your responsibility to meet with the class instructor in advance to request arrangements related to your religious observances that may conflict with this class, and to make appropriate plans to make up any missed work. The following is a link from the Chaplain’s Office website where a list of Religious Holidays needing accommodations (if requested) is posted: https://www.etown.edu/offices/chaplain/index.aspx
Mental Health and Counseling Resources Counseling Services provides a broad range of counseling and mental health support services that facilitate students’ personal, social, and academic development. The licensed mental health professionals provide short-term individual counseling, group counseling, crisis intervention, and consultation to currently enrolled students for no additional charge. Counseling services are provided in a confidential and diversity-affirming environment to help students address a variety of mental health, situational, and developmental concerns. The office is located in the Baugher Student Center, Suite 216. Appointments can be made in person or by calling 717-361-1405. Urgent walk-in services are also available. To access the after-hours crisis services, please call the 24/7 Campus Security number of 717-361-1111. For more information, please visit www.etown.edu/offices/counseling.
ADA Statement Elizabethtown College is committed to providing access for all students to courses, programs, services, and activities. If you have a documented disability such as a learning disability, chronic illness, or a new circumstance such as a concussion and would like to request accommodations, contact Dr. Michele Moohr, Coordinator of Disability Services by phone (717-361-1227) or e-mail (moohrm@etown.edu). The Office of Disability Services can provide resources to you and facilitate communication with faculty about reasonable accommodations. After meeting with the Office of Disability Services, students must set up an appointment to meet with me, the instructor, to discuss the accommodations as they pertain to my class. Common accommodations may include extra time on exams, an alternate exam location, the ability to record class lectures, and access to content with a screen reader.
Modifications for Non-native English Speakers Elizabethtown College is committed to providing equitable access to all courses, programs, and services for non-native (international and domestic) English speakers. Students may request tutoring, learning resources, course modifications, and learning opportunities. Students interested in seeking a course modification should contact Ms. Maria Petty (pettym@etown.edu), International Student Programs Advisor, at (717) 361-1594.
Title IX Elizabethtown College and its faculty are committed to creating a safe and open learning environment for all students. If you or someone you know has experienced sexual harassment, including sexual assault, dating or domestic violence, and stalking, please know that help and support are available. Etown strongly encourages all members of the community to take action, seek support, and report incidents of sexual harassment to the Title IX Office. You may contact the Title IX Coordinator at reedg@etown.edu or learn more by visiting https://www.etown.edu/offices/diversity/titleix/index.aspx. Please be aware that faculty members are required to disclose information about suspected or alleged sexual harassment or other potential violations of the College Sexual Misconduct Policies and Procedures to the Title IX Coordinator. If the Title IX Coordinator receives information about an incident, they will reach out to offer information about resources, rights, and procedural options as a member of the campus community. Community members are not required to respond to this outreach. If you, or another student you know, wishes to speak to a confidential resource who does not have this reporting responsibility, please contact Counseling Services at 717-361-1405.

Students are responsible for checking the schedule regularly. Schedule page will include: 1) teaching topics for each meeting; 2) reading assignments for each week and 3) special notes on specific days.
Course Announcements & Discussion All course announcements will be sent to your E-Town email accounts via Canvas Announcements. You are responsible for signing up for this service and checking your emails regularly.
I have created a Microsoft Teams channel (link) to facilitate course related discussion. Discussions are encouraged to be posted on the “QA” channel from Teams. Private instant messages can be sent directly to your recipient by search your recipient’s name on the “search” bar.
Attendance Policies Attendance is expected of every student at every lecture. Students are responsible for all content covered in class as well as assigned book chapters. Due to their nature, pop quizzes cannot be made up.
Except in the case of documented emergencies, neither exams nor in-class labs can be made up afterwards. For excused absences, students must arrange to take the exam or do the lab before the normally scheduled time. Arrangements must be made with the instructor at least two weeks prior to the scheduled time.
Students are expected to maintain an attitude of respect at all times toward their colleagues, the equipment, and the instructor. Cell phones and similar devices is prohibited from using during lecturing time. Students who use offensive language, misuse computing facilities, or are otherwise disruptive of the classroom will be asked to leave.
Statement on School Closure In the event that classes do not meet because Elizabethtown College is closed or delayed due to inclement weather or some other emergency, the slides that would have been covered during the missed classes will be posted through Canvas. Students are expected to do the assigned reading, review the slides, and e-mail the instructor with any questions. There will also be an opportunity to ask questions about the material when classes resume.
If a scheduled exam or lab is missed, it will normally be made up on the day that classes resume. If the College is closed on a day when a project is due, the project due date will also normally be extended until the day when classes resume. If circumstances render either of these makeup policies unreasonable, the instructor will send an e-mail explaining an alternative makeup opportunity to each student’s Elizabethtown e-mail account.
Statement on Academic Integrity Check out the up-to-date statement from: Elizabethtown College Catalog, “Academic Judicial System”
Statement on the Use of ChatGPT and Generative AI Tools The use of GenAI tools like ChatGPT to generate source code is prohibited for your assignments in this course unless otherwise noted in the syllabus. Therefore, your instructor will consider it a violation of academic integrity to use a GenAI tool for any purpose that is not explicitly outlined in assignment instructions. While this new technology can be very useful in certain contexts, it is important to make sure that its usage in the classroom setting is limited in order to ensure that you are doing original work and developing your critical thinking skills. In circumstances in which AI usage is permitted in class, you must acknowledge that usage and provide the chatbot with credit when it is a cited source. For instance, to cite ChatGPT in APA, the APA provides some direction at https://apastyle.apa.org/blog/how-to-cite-chatgpt. If you have any questions or uncertainty over the use of AI in this course, please reach out to the instructor.
Respect for Diversity It is my intent that students from all backgrounds and perspectives be well served by this course, that students’ learning needs be addressed both in and out of class, and that the diversity that students bring to this class be viewed as a resource, strength, and benefit. I also intend to present materials and activities that respect diversity: gender, sexuality, disability, age, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, race, and culture. Please let me know if there are ways to further serve the diverse needs you or other students may have.
Religious Observances The College is eager to facilitate individual religious beliefs and practices whenever possible while retaining course student learning outcomes. It is your responsibility to meet with the class instructor in advance to request arrangements related to your religious observances that may conflict with this class, and to make appropriate plans to make up any missed work. The following is a link from the Chaplain’s Office website where a list of Religious Holidays needing accommodations (if requested) is posted: https://www.etown.edu/offices/chaplain/index.aspx
Mental Health and Counseling Resources Counseling Services provides a broad range of counseling and mental health support services that facilitate students’ personal, social, and academic development. The licensed mental health professionals provide short-term individual counseling, group counseling, crisis intervention, and consultation to currently enrolled students for no additional charge. Counseling services are provided in a confidential and diversity-affirming environment to help students address a variety of mental health, situational, and developmental concerns. The office is located in the Baugher Student Center, Suite 216. Appointments can be made in person or by calling 717-361-1405. Urgent walk-in services are also available. To access the after-hours crisis services, please call the 24/7 Campus Security number of 717-361-1111. For more information, please visit www.etown.edu/offices/counseling.
ADA Statement Elizabethtown College is committed to providing access for all students to courses, programs, services, and activities. If you have a documented disability such as a learning disability, chronic illness, or a new circumstance such as a concussion and would like to request accommodations, contact Dr. Michele Moohr, Coordinator of Disability Services by phone (717-361-1227) or e-mail (moohrm@etown.edu). The Office of Disability Services can provide resources to you and facilitate communication with faculty about reasonable accommodations. After meeting with the Office of Disability Services, students must set up an appointment to meet with me, the instructor, to discuss the accommodations as they pertain to my class. Common accommodations may include extra time on exams, an alternate exam location, the ability to record class lectures, and access to content with a screen reader.
Modifications for Non-native English Speakers Elizabethtown College is committed to providing equitable access to all courses, programs, and services for non-native (international and domestic) English speakers. Students may request tutoring, learning resources, course modifications, and learning opportunities. Students interested in seeking a course modification should contact Ms. Maria Petty (pettym@etown.edu), International Student Programs Advisor, at (717) 361-1594.
Title IX Elizabethtown College and its faculty are committed to creating a safe and open learning environment for all students. If you or someone you know has experienced sexual harassment, including sexual assault, dating or domestic violence, and stalking, please know that help and support are available. Etown strongly encourages all members of the community to take action, seek support, and report incidents of sexual harassment to the Title IX Office. You may contact the Title IX Coordinator at reedg@etown.edu or learn more by visiting https://www.etown.edu/offices/diversity/titleix/index.aspx. Please be aware that faculty members are required to disclose information about suspected or alleged sexual harassment or other potential violations of the College Sexual Misconduct Policies and Procedures to the Title IX Coordinator. If the Title IX Coordinator receives information about an incident, they will reach out to offer information about resources, rights, and procedural options as a member of the campus community. Community members are not required to respond to this outreach. If you, or another student you know, wishes to speak to a confidential resource who does not have this reporting responsibility, please contact Counseling Services at 717-361-1405.

content:
Grading Weights The final grade for this course depends upon the grades and scores earned on course components weighted as follows:
 3%: Persistence. Attendance and in-class question answering. 6%: A number of in-class pop quizzes. 18%: 6 individual homework. 18%: 3 team projects. 20%: 5 in-class labs. 15%: Midterm exam. 20%: Final exam.  Grades will be computed by rounding numerical percentages to the nearest integer and applying the following table:
   Letter Range Letter Range Letter Range     A 93-100 B- 80-82 D+ 67-69   A- 90-92 C+ 77-79 D 63-66   B+ 87-89 C 73-76 D- 60-62   B 83-86 C- 70-72 F 0-59     In-class Labs All labs are to be done individually, in class, with the assistance of the instructor. Each assignment will be given near the beginning of a class and must be uploaded to Canvas (https://etown.instructure.com/) before the end of the class without late penalty. Extended submission is due on the same day before midnight, but any submission during this grace period will receive 15 points (out of 100) of late penalty. Submissions beyond midnight the same day will not be accepted. To receive full credit, a programming assignment must run without exceptions (errors), but partial credit will be awarded based on the understanding of the material demonstrated by the student’s code.
Homework All homework assignments have to be completed individually in this course. Typically, you will have about two weeks to complete each assignment.
Projects All projects are team projects in this course. For each project, all students must form teams of 2-3 members. Students should select their teams by using the Groups tab under People, on the Canvas webpage.
Teams are responsible for dividing their workload and meeting offline for at least 3 times. Documented meeting minutes have to be submitted as part of the deliverable. Except under extreme circumstances, all members of the team will receive the same grade for each project. One member of each team is designated the leader. The files for each project should be zipped up and uploaded by the team leader using Canvas before the due date.
Project and Homework Grading and Late Policy All homework and project assignments will be graded based on the following criteria:
 Correctness: Finding the right answer Formatting:	Displaying the right answer according to instructions Style and Documentation: Producing readable code with appropriate comments  In general, assignments will be graded with the diff utility. For that reason, it is imperative that project output matches sample output to the character.
Late assignment will lose points per day, including weekends and holidays. For example, -1 after 1 day, -2 after 2 days, -4 after 3 days … until 8+ days students will receive 0 score. Under no circumstances should any student disclose their code, or copy the code written by other students or from an outside source. Both students will receive 0 score on the disclosed/copied assignment.

This system emphasizes total team mastery, rewarding the fastest successful group with “Gold Status” exam points and allowing Clans to “boot” non-contributing members via a 60% majority vote. For more details, read on.
1. Clan Formation & Leadership  Structure: Each Clan consists of one Leader and 3–4 Members. The Draft (Quiz 0): On Day 1, students complete Quiz 0 to nominate a Leader and a Co-leader. Self-nominations are allowed. Succession:  In the event of a tie, the Instructor decides. The runner-up becomes the Co-leader. If the primary Leader is disqualified (e.g., fails an audit or loses status), the Co-leader automatically assumes the role and perks.    2. The “Gatekeeper” Perks Leaders are the backbone of the course. In recognition of their workload, they receive:
 The Prestige Perk: A one-letter grade increase on the final weighted grade (e.g., B → A). Leadership Endorsement: A formal recommendation letter from the Instructor upon request for any positions. The Qualification Requirement:  Leaders must pass their own Check-off with a Coach/Instructor one week prior to each project deadline. Failure to qualify results in demotion to Co-leader.    3. The Member Sign-Off Process Once a Leader is qualified, they check off members using a Digital Sign-Off Card (MS Forms).
 Explanation Phase: The member presents a truth table and a hand-drawn diagram. Stress Test: The Leader asks Instructor-provided “what-if” logic questions. Validity Window: Sign-offs are valid only until one week after the project due date. Accountability:  If a Leader signs off on a student who later fails an Instructor Audit, the Leader permanently loses Leader status.    4. The Raid: Random Audit Grading Once the Clan is marked Ready, the Raid begins:
 Selection: The Instructor/Coach randomly selects 1–2 signed-off members (excluding booted members) for a face-to-face explanation. The Win: If the selected member(s) pass, the entire Clan earns 100%. The Risk (Grade Cap):  If a selected member fails, the entire Clan’s grade is capped at that member’s demonstrated performance level
(e.g., 60% mastery → Clan grade capped at 60%).    5. The Booting Policy: Clan Protection To prevent inactive members from jeopardizing the Clan’s audit grade, Clans may remove members.
 Requirement: A booting request must be approved by more than 60% of the Clan
(e.g., 3 of 4 members, or 3 of 5). Process:  The Leader submits an official Booting Request Email to the Instructor describing the member’s lack of participation or mastery.   Instructor Audit:  The Instructor investigates. If approved, the booted member is excluded from the Clan’s Random Audit for that project.   Consequences:  The booted member receives 0% for the project. To rejoin the Clan for the next project, the student must demonstrate 100% mastery of the missed content to the Instructor in a private session before the next project starts.    6. Gold Status (The Speed Bonus)  Reward: For each project, the first Clan to submit a flawless package and complete all sign-offs earns Gold Status. Perk: +2 extra points on the next exam for all Clan members. The Steal:  If a Gold Status Clan fails its Audit, the status is revoked and awarded to the next fastest successful Clan.    7. Grading Rubric: The Raid Audit    Performance Level Requirement for the Randomly Selected Member Clan Result     Mastery (100%) Explains the gate logic, truth table, and passes the Stress Test flawlessly. Full Credit (100%)   Proficient (85%) Understands the general logic but misses one nuance in the stress test. Grade capped at 85%   Developing (70%) Can show working code but struggles to explain the hand-drawn diagram. Grade capped at 70%   Unsatisfactory (<50%) Cannot explain the logic or truth table; clear evidence of copying. Zero Credit / Academic Integrity Review

content:
Code Grading rubrics for code submission in terms of percentage:
100%:  Functionality: For assignments that have well-specified behavior, the code should be able to pass (or very nearly pass, e.g. there may be minor output formatting issues) automated unit testing of all required features. For open-ended assignments the code must be easy to run without modification and implement all of the required functionality. Documentation: all functions are commented with appropriate doc strings. For open-ended assignments there is a README file discussing how to run the program and what it is supposed to do. Style: the program exhibits effective modular design. The code does not have unnecessary cut and paste code or magic numbers. Variable and function names are sensibly chosen.  80%:  Functionality: For assignments that have well-specified behavior, the code should implement all of the required functionality. For this grade, it is possible that 10-20% of the functionality may be broken. For open-ended assignments it will be possible to get the code running with modest effort (i.e. it will not be as well documented as in a 5, but it isn’t too hard to intuit how the code works). For these types of assignments all required features must be present, however, some (10-20%) may not be functioning properly or otherwise poorly implemented. Documentation: some functions are missing doc strings. Comments are fairly minimal. Style: some aspects of the design of the program could be improved to reduce cut and paste code. Variable and function names are for the most part well-chosen.  60%:  Functionality: The code should implement almost all of the required features (it is okay if roughly 20% are not implemented). A significant portion, 30-50%, of the code may not work as it is supposed to. Documentation: Docstrings are mostly absent For well-defined assignments the code does not run as it should based on the assignment spec. For open-ended assignments there may not be any indication of how to run the program, and it is not easy for a NINJA to figure out how the code works (a good test is if you have to e-mail someone to ask them how their code runs, they are probably at this level). Style: the program design needs improvement. The code would be a lot cleaner if the author had done a better job thinking through the appropriate functional decomposition. The code has lots of cut and paste and magic numbers. Variable and function names are hard to interpret.  40%:  Functionality: the assignment is incomplete (~50% of the functionality is not implemented). The functionality that is implemented is not 100% correct. Documentation: mostly absent. Style: design is poor. Very little attention has been paid to choosing a sensible functional decomposition. Variable and function names are chosen almost arbitrarily.  20%:  Functionality: only minimal functionality is present. Documentation: little or none. Style: Code is not “readable”. Poor choice of variable and function names.  0%:  nothing turned in.  Notebook Assignments Jupyter notebooks are the files you need to submit for labs and homework assignments.
100%: Thorough engagement with each section of the reading. Each exercise has either been completed, or you have articulated a well-thought out set of questions for each of the problems you didn’t answer. Points will be deducted from 100% for the following reasons:
 Exercises are not filled out (either with a solution or a question) The answer to the exercise does not demonstrate a good faith attempt to complete it.  Writing Writing will be evaluated for clarity, concision, and comprehensiveness. The particular style that you should use will depend on the assignment and your audience. The bottom line is don’t cut corners with writing in this class. Your ability to communicate what you have done is just as important as what you have done. Don’t make the mistake of spending all of your time writing code, and then rush through the writing parts of the assignment. See below for some stylistic guidance.
 Since the dawn of time, college students have been writing introductions that are too grandiose (and often false). Just get into it; you don’t have to zoom in from space (and make stuff up). Write the abstract last and summarize the most important result. The passive voice is a hoax. Please write in the first person (singular or plural). Write in the present tense whenever possible. Some actions happen in the past, but all research exists in an eternal present: “Using data from BRFSS, they plot weight versus height and find that tall respondents are heavier, on average, than shorter respondents. Our results are consistent with this conclusion.” When you edit, try to remove words. Avoid using “significant” unless you mean “statistically significant;” a good alternative is “substantial.” Avoid using “correlation” unless you mean a coefficient of correlation. In general, there might be a “relationship” between variables and you might characterize it with a correlation. “Trend” usually means something is changing in time; “pattern” is more general. Provide indicators of logical flow. If I ask you to answer a set of question in your report, don’t just paste the questions as your section headings. You should create your own document structure based on what makes sense for your project. Explain your motivation. Avoid “We were interested” and “We wanted” as pseudo-motivation. And don’t look at the camera; that is, don’t use “because we were told to” as motivation, and avoid “for this project”. When you refer to figures and tables, capitalize “Figure” and “Table.” Formal figures have a number and a caption, and they can float. Informal figures are part of the text flow. If a figure doesn’t contain much information, summarize it in text. Find an authorial voice that is casual enough to be engaging (without overdoing it).

content: What you just did Computers store every number as a row of on/off switches called bits. Each switch is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on up to 128. Eight of them together make a byte, which can hold any whole number from 0 to 255. The row of 0s and 1s under the number is that byte, written the way a computer stores it. So when you made 37, you wrote 00100101, which is 37 in binary.
summary: A one-minute game about how computers count. Flip the switches so they add up to the number.

How a map app finds the fastest route The shortest-looking route is often not the fastest one, which is why map apps don’t just pick the path with the fewest turns. They use a method worked out by the computer scientist Edsger Dijkstra in 1956 and published in 1959.
It works like this: start where you are, at 0 minutes. Then, again and again, take the closest place whose time isn’t final yet, mark its time as final, and see whether going through it gives any of its neighbors a faster time. When the destination’s time becomes final, it is guaranteed to be the fastest possible. Press Watch a computer solve it after a puzzle to see each step on the map.
summary: A daily puzzle: find the fastest walk across the Elizabethtown College campus. Everyone gets the same route each day, and practice routes are unlimited.

title: Code Word

content:
What the gates do Every decision a computer makes is built from tiny circuits like this one. Each gate takes signals that are on or off and passes on a new one: AND is on only when both of its inputs are on, OR is on when at least one is, NOT flips its input, and XOR (from Friday on) is on when exactly one input is on. A computer’s processor is built from gates like these, made of billions of tiny electronic switches called transistors.
Why “Watch a computer solve it” matters A computer can simply try every combination of switches: with 6 switches there are only 64. But each extra switch doubles the count, so with 30 switches there would be over a billion combinations. Telling which circuits can ever be switched on is a famous hard problem in computer science, and much of the field is about finding cleverer ways than trying everything.
summary: A daily circuit puzzle: flip switches to light the bulb using as few switches as possible.
title: Logic Lights

content:
How the code works Each day’s quotation is written in a substitution cipher: every letter is swapped for another letter, and the same letter is always swapped the same way. Spaces and punctuation stay put. If Q stands for E once, it stands for E everywhere.
How to crack it Start with what you know about English. Short words help: a one-letter word is almost always A or I, and three-letter words are often THE or AND. Letter counts help even more: E, T, A, O, I and N are the most common letters in English, so the most common letters in the puzzle are good first guesses. Counting letters to break a code is called frequency analysis, and the Arab scholar al-Kindi described it in the 9th century.
Every quotation comes from a book in the public domain and was checked word for word against the book’s text at Project Gutenberg.
summary: A daily puzzle: a quotation from a classic book is scrambled letter by letter. Work out the code to read it.
title: Crack the Cipher

content:
Exam schedules are a coloring puzzle Every college has to fit its final exams into a few time slots so that no student has two exams at once. Computer scientists draw this as a graph: each course is a dot, and a line joins two courses that share a student. Giving every course a slot so that no line joins two courses in the same slot is called graph coloring, because the slots are usually drawn as colors. In 1967 the mathematicians Dominic Welsh and Martin Powell showed how a simple coloring method applies to timetabling, and scheduling software still builds on ideas like theirs.
Why the fewest slots is hard to find Checking a finished schedule is easy: look at every line. Finding one with the fewest slots is another matter. In 1972 Richard Karp showed that this problem belongs to a large family of problems for which nobody knows a fast method, and it is still one of computing’s famous hard problems. With a few hundred courses, trying every schedule is out of reach, so real scheduling software uses clever shortcuts that find good answers, not always the best one.
Four slots are always enough here These puzzles are drawn so that no two lines cross. For any drawing like that, four slots are always enough. This is the Four Color Theorem, first asked about maps in 1852 and proved in 1976 by Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken: the first major theorem proved with the help of a computer. Real exam schedules have lines crossing everywhere, so they can need many more slots.
summary: A daily scheduling puzzle: fit every exam into the fewest time slots so that no student has two exams at once.

content:
Part 3 of 9 in the series AI at a Small College.
Course planning is where AI earns its keep for most faculty. It is also where its mistakes are easiest to miss. In the California State University system’s fall 2025 survey, developing course materials was the most common way faculty used AI, at 55%. This post gives a routine that works in any discipline, whether you teach organic chemistry, first-year writing or a studio course. It follows the familiar “backward design” order:
 Decide what students should be able to do. Decide how you will know they can do it. Plan the weeks.  AI drafts each step; you decide.
Step 1: Set up a course workspace (15 minutes, once) Most licensed AI tools now let you save instructions and files in one place, so you don’t start from scratch each time. Depending on what your college offers, that place might be a NotebookLM notebook, a Gemini Gem, a ChatGPT project or custom GPT, a Claude project or a Copilot notebook.
Create one for the course and add:
 the catalog description and any department or general-education outcomes the course must meet; your last syllabus and schedule, if you have taught it before; your own notes on what worked and what did not; openly licensed or library-provided readings you already plan to use.  Do not add student work, grades or student comments (see Part 2).
Then paste in standing instructions, so every request follows the same rules:
You are helping me plan [COURSE NAME], a [level, e.g., 200-level] course in [discipline] for [who takes it, e.g., sophomores, mostly non-majors] at a small liberal arts college. Work only from the files I provided and what I tell you. Never invent readings, citations, page numbers, dates or college policies. When you need one, write [READING NEEDED], [DATE NEEDED] or [POLICY NEEDED] instead. Keep suggestions realistic for a class of [number] students meeting [days and length]. Ask me a question if something is unclear.  Step 2: Draft learning goals (15 minutes) Draft 5 to 7 learning outcomes for this course. Each must start with an observable verb (analyze, design, compare, explain, create...), fit the catalog description, and be something a student could show in [the number of weeks] weeks. For each outcome, add one sentence on how a student would demonstrate it. Mark which outcomes cover the department or general-education outcomes in my files.  Read the list against your own sense of the course. Expect to rewrite. The value is a structured starting point and options you might not have considered, not a finished answer. Cut anything that sounds generic, such as “develop critical thinking skills”, unless you can say exactly how students will show it.
Step 3: Align assignments to the goals (20 minutes) For the outcomes I approved (pasted below), propose a set of assessments for the semester. For each, give: which outcomes it measures, format, approximate student hours, and when in the term it fits. Include at least one assessment that students complete in class or explain orally, so it shows their own understanding. Finish with a table: rows = outcomes, columns = assessments, cells = how strongly each assessment measures each outcome.  That last table, an alignment map, is the most useful thing in this step. It shows outcomes that nothing measures and assignments that measure nothing you care about. Check the student-hours column against your college’s credit-hour expectations. AI is often optimistic about how long things take.
Step 4: Map the weeks, but do the dates yourself AI tools are unreliable at calendar arithmetic, such as which weekday a holiday falls on or how many class meetings fit before break. So build the calendar first:
 Open your college’s academic calendar. Type every class meeting date into a simple table in a document or spreadsheet, and mark holidays and breaks.  Then ask AI only to fill topics into the rows you made:
Here is my table of class meetings (dates already filled in; do not change them). Fill in the Topic and Preparation columns so the course builds toward the assessments in the order I approved. Keep one main topic per meeting. Put [READING NEEDED] wherever a reading should go. Leave the rows marked BREAK empty.  Step 5: Find readings yourself Never accept a citation an AI suggests without finding the source yourself. In a 2025 study, GPT-4o fabricated almost 1 in 5 of the references it produced, and fabrication was worse on specialized topics, which is exactly where faculty need help. Ask instead for search terms and the kinds of sources to look for:
For each [READING NEEDED] slot, suggest 3 search phrases I could use in our library databases and the type of source that would fit (primary source, review article, textbook chapter, case study, dataset). Do not name specific titles or authors.  Then search your library’s databases or ask your subject librarian. Only list what you have actually opened.
Step 6: Write the policies in your own voice AI can draft standard syllabus sections such as attendance, late work and accessibility. Start from your college’s required syllabus language. Your AI-use policy for students is worth writing yourself, because it signals what you value. A useful structure:
 Where AI is welcome. Where it is not. How students should disclose AI use. What happens if they don’t.  Step 7: Keep it yours According to the US Copyright Office, prompts alone don’t make you the author of what AI generates, but your selection, arrangement and revision can be protected. Beyond copyright, the course should sound like you. Keep a short “changes” note as you edit: what you cut, rewrote or added. That note also becomes your starting point next year.
Next year: revise from evidence At the end of the term, add to the workspace:
 your “changes” note; your reflections; aggregate results only, such as which quiz questions most students missed, or the three most common themes in course evaluations, with no names and no quotes from small classes.  Then ask:
Using my notes and these aggregate results, suggest the three revisions most likely to improve student learning next term. For each, say which outcome it serves, what evidence in my files supports it, and what it would cost me in preparation time.  Try it this week  Pick a course you will teach next term. Do Steps 1 to 3. Plan on about 50 minutes. Compare the alignment map with your current syllabus. Find one outcome that nothing measures well, or one assignment that doesn’t map to any outcome. Write down the minutes it took, and whether the result was better than what you would have done alone.  Next time: making quizzes, handouts and slides with AI, and catching the specific mistakes AI tends to make.
Have a planning prompt that works well in your discipline? Send it to me at lip AT etown DOT edu, and I may include it in a later post.
Sources  Inside Higher Ed, California State University faculty AI survey (fall 2025) UConn eCampus, Backward design with AI JMIR, Citation fabrication by GPT-4o (2025) US Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability (2025)
summary: A step-by-step routine for using AI as a planning partner: write learning goals, align assignments to them, map the weeks and find readings, with the checks that keep the result yours and correct.
